Multivariable models currently comprise a large proportion of indexed radiological literature but authors' motivation to develop and publish models, available resource, plans for external evaluation, and whether models are used, is generally unknown. Statistical assistance was largely absent or minimal. [PMID 42898001] (The British journal of radiology, 2026) Why do authors publish radiological multivariable models: Questionnaire survey of motivations, evaluation, and usage in clinical practice. Multivariable models currently comprise a large proportion of indexed radiological literature but authors' motivation to develop and publish models, available resource, plans for external evaluation, and whether models are used, is generally unknown. We aimed to answer these questions via a questionnaire survey. We administered an online questionnaire to authors reporting multivariable prognostic or diagnostic models developed using regression, published in the top 3 indexed general radiological journals 2013 to 2015 and December 2022 to May 2023 inclusive. 34 authors responded. Regarding external evaluation, the most frequent response (49%, 17/35 responses) stated no intention to do this. Regarding barriers to evaluation, respondents cited lack of time (27%, 18/67 responses; multiple responses were possible), funding (22%, n = 15), and interest in development alone (19%, n = 13). 67% (n = 23) declared no or little statistical support. Most (82%, n = 28) did not use their own model in clinical practice and most (56%, n = 19) also believed other clinicians would not use the model either. Most (79%, n = 27) did not use models in general. A substantial proportion (29%, n = 10) reported model development to progress their career via publication. Most respondents had neither evaluated their model nor intended to do so. Most did not use their own model in clinical practice, nor did they believe others would. Statistical assistance was largely absent or minimal. Our data suggest that the large volume of multivariable models currently available in the indexed medical literature have little clinical utility.

[PMID 42898001] (The British journal of radiology, 2026) Why do authors publish radiological multivariable models: Questionnaire survey of motivations, evaluation, and usage in clinical practice. Multivariable models currently comprise a large proportion of indexed radiological literature but authors' motivation to develop and publish models, available resource, plans for external evaluation, and whether models are used, is generally unknown. We aimed to answer these questions via a questionnaire survey. We administered an online questionnaire to authors reporting multivariable prognostic or diagnostic models developed using regression, published in the top 3 indexed general radiological journals 2013 to 2015 and December 2022 to May 2023 inclusive. 34 authors responded. Statistical assistance was largely absent or minimal. [PMID 42898001] (The British journal of radiology, 2026) Why do authors publish radiological multivariable models: Questionnaire survey of motivations, evaluation, and usage in clinical practice. Multivariable models currently comprise a large proportion of indexed radiological literature but authors' motivation to develop and publish models, available resource, plans for external evaluation, and whether models are used, is generally unknown. We aimed to answer these questions via a questionnaire survey. We administered an online questionnaire to authors reporting multivariable prognostic or diagnostic models developed using regression, published in the top 3 indexed general radiological journals 2013 to 2015 and December 2022 to May 2023 inclusive. 34 authors responded. Regarding external evaluation, the most frequent response (49%, 17/35 responses) stated no intention to do this. Regarding barriers to evaluation, respondents cited lack of time (27%, 18/67 responses; multiple responses were possible), funding (22%, n = 15), and interest in development alone (19%, n = 13). 67% (n = 23) declared no or little statistical support. Most (82%, n = 28) did not use their own model in clinical practice and most (56%, n = 19) also believed other clinicians would not use the model either. Most (79%, n = 27) did not use models in general. A substantial proportion (29%, n = 10) reported model development to progress their career via publication. Most respondents had neither evaluated their model nor intended to do so. Most did not use their own model in clinical practice, nor did they believe others would. Statistical assistance was largely absent or minimal. Our data suggest that the large volume of multivariable models currently available in the indexed medical literature have little clinical utility.

Altered cholesterol homeostasis in cystic fibrosis patients has been reported, although controversy remains. As a major membrane lipid component, cholesterol modulates the function of multiple ion channels by complicated mechanisms. However, whether cholesterol directly modulates cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel function remains unknown. To answer this question, we determined the effects of changing plasma membrane cholesterol levels on CFTR channel function utilizing polarized fischer rat thyroid (FRT) cells and primary human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cells. Treatment with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) significantly reduced total cholesterol content in FRT cells, which significantly decreased forskolin (FSK)-mediated activation of both wildtype (WT-) and P67L-CFTR. This effect was also seen in HBE cells expressing WT-CFTR. Cholesterol modification by cholesterol oxidase and cholesterol esterase also distinctly affected activation of CFTR by FSK. In addition, alteration of cholesterol increased the potency of VX-770, a clinically used potentiator of CFTR, when both WT- and P67L-CFTR channels were activated at low FSK concentrations; this likely reflects the apparent shift in the sensitivity of WT-CFTR to FSK after alteration of membrane cholesterol. These results demonstrate that changes in the plasma membrane cholesterol level significantly modulate CFTR channel function and consequently may affect sensitivity to clinical therapeutics in CF patients.

Circulation 116, 2563-2570 (2007). Warfarin is an effective oral anticoagulant used to treat or prevent thromboembolic disorders in millions of patients worldwide. Even with conscientious International Normalized Ratio (INR) monitoring, warfarin initiation carries a high risk of hemorrhage. Pharmacogenetic studies have determined that variants in the CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genes help to predict the therapeutic warfarin dose. Whether using this information prospectively will prevent under- and over-dosing of warfarin is unknown. To answer this question, the Couma-Gen investigators randomized half of a 200-patient cohort beginning warfarin therapy to clinical dosing and half to pharmacogenetic dosing. Overall, pharmacogenetic dosing slightly increased time in the therapeutic INR range (p = not significant) and decreased the number of INR tests required. The trial has important implications for the new NIH-funded multicentered trial. Here, we discuss the Couma-Gen study and its implications for the design, randomization, blinding and end point definition of future studies.

[PMID 42907420] (The American surgeon, 2026) When Representation Is Not Enough: Persistent Gender Discrimination in a Majority-Women Surgical Workforce. BackgroundGender-based discrimination affects up to 50% of early-career surgeons in high-income countries. We carried out this study to examine gender-based discrimination in surgical fraternities within the Commonwealth Caribbean.MethodologyResearchers interviewed active physician members of the surgical fraternity who were registered with the medical councils in 17 nations in the Commonwealth Caribbean. A validated questionnaire was used to collect data on gender-based discrimination and unprofessional behavior in the workplace.ResultsData were collected from 190 participants, composed of 76 (40%) men and 114 (60%) women. There were 67/190 (35%) respondents who experienced gender-based discrimination. After multivariate logistic regression analysis, gender (adjusted odds ratio: 5.59; CI: 2.55-12.26; P < 0.001) and training level (adjusted odds ratio: 1.94; CI: 1.01-3.74; P 0.048) were independent predictors of experiencing gender-based discrimination. Seventy-one (37%) participants declined to answer questions about unprofessional behavior, and women were over-represented in non-responders (49% vs 20%; P < 0.001), creating the potential for selection bias in unknown directions, and potentially altering prevalence and associations in 119 respondents. Firth penalized likelihood logistic regression models were used to compensate for data sparsity and quasi-complete separation as only 4/61 (6.6%) males experienced unprofessional behavior. This revealed that gender (adjusted odds ratio: 24.70; CI: 8.72-69-.96; P < 0.001), but not training levels, remained a significant predictor of unprofessional behavior.ConclusionThis study demonstrates that respondents within the surveyed surgical fraternity continued to experience discrimination and unprofessional behavior, despite women surgeons accounting for the numerical majori
[PMID 42898001] (The British journal of radiology, 2026) Why do authors publish radiological multivariable models: Questionnaire survey of motivations, evaluation, and usage in clinical practice. Multivariable models currently comprise a large proportion of indexed radiological literature but authors' motivation to develop and publish models, available resource, plans for external evaluation, and whether models are used, is generally unknown. We aimed to answer these questions via a questionnaire survey. We administered an online questionnaire to authors reporting multivariable prognostic or diagnostic models developed using regression, published in the top 3 indexed general radiological journals 2013 to 2015 and December 2022 to May 2023 inclusive. 34 authors responded. Regarding external evaluation, the most frequent response (49%, 17/35 responses) stated no intention to do this. Regarding barriers to evaluation, respondents cited lack of time (27%, 18/67 responses; multiple responses were possible), funding (22%, n = 15), and interest in development alone (19%, n = 13). 67% (n = 23) declared no or little statistical support. Most (82%, n = 28) did not use their own model in clinical practice and most (56%, n = 19) also believed other clinicians would not use the model either. Most (79%, n = 27) did not use models in general. A substantial proportion (29%, n = 10) reported model development to progress their career via publication. Most respondents had neither evaluated their model nor intended to do so. Most did not use their own model in clinical practice, nor did they believe others would. Statistical assistance was largely absent or minimal. Our data suggest that the large volume of multivariable models currently available in the indexed medical literature have little clinical utility.

generated_answer: Warfarin-induced adverse reactions are significantly influenced by genetic variations in CYP2C9 and VKORC1. Variants in these genes affect warfarin metabolism and sensitivity, respectively, leading to inter-individual variability in therapeutic response and risk of bleeding or thromboembolic events. reasoning: Warfarin is metabolized by CYP2C9 and its effectiveness is affected by VKORC1. Variants in these genes can influence the therapeutic dose of warfarin, as they affect how quickly a patient will process the drug (CYP2C9) and their sensitivity to it (VKORC1). Therefore, when initiating warfarin therapy, it is advisable to include CYP2C9 and VKORC1 in a pharmacogenetics panel. This helps predict the appropriate dose of warfarin for individual patients, potentially reducing the risk of hemorrhage or thromboembolic events due to under- or over-dosing.
search_context: [PMID 29783347] (Personalized medicine, 2008) Couma-Gen: implications for future randomized trials of pharmacogenetic-based warfarin therapy. Evaluation of: Anderson JL, Horne BD, Stevens SM et al.: Randomized trial of genotype-guided versus standard warfarin dosing in patients initiating oral anticoagulation. Circulation 116, 2563-2570 (2007). Warfarin is an effective oral anticoagulant used to treat or prevent thromboembolic disorders in millions of patients worldwide. Even with conscientious International Normalized Ratio (INR) monitoring, warfarin initiation carries a high risk of hemorrhage. Pharmacogenetic studies have determined that variants in the CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genes help to predict the therapeutic warfarin dose. Whether using this information prospectively will prevent under- and over-dosing of warfarin is unknown. To answer this question, the Couma-Gen investigators randomized half of a 200-patient cohort beginning warfarin therapy to clinical dosing and half to pharmacogenetic dosing. Overall, pharmacogenetic dosing slightly increased time in the therapeutic INR range (p = not significant) and decreased the number of INR tests required. The trial has important implications for the new NIH-funded multicentered trial. Here, we discuss the Couma-Gen study and its implications for the design, randomization, blinding and end point definition of future studies.

Additionally, other genes such as ABCB1 (which encodes the P-glycoprotein transporter) may also be considered due to its role in the transport of pantoprazole across cell membranes and into the bloodstream. However, based on current knowledge, CYP2C19 is the primary gene to include.

[PMID 42898001] (The British journal of radiology, 2026) Why do authors publish radiological multivariable models: Questionnaire survey of motivations, evaluation, and usage in clinical practice. Multivariable models currently comprise a large proportion of indexed radiological literature but authors' motivation to develop and publish models, available resource, plans for external evaluation, and whether models are used, is generally unknown. We aimed to answer these questions via a questionnaire survey. We administered an online questionnaire to authors reporting multivariable prognostic or diagnostic models developed using regression, published in the top 3 indexed general radiological journals 2013 to 2015 and December 2022 to May 2023 inclusive. 34 authors responded. Regarding external evaluation, the most frequent response (49%, 17/35 responses) stated no intention to do this. Regarding barriers to evaluation, respondents cited lack of time (27%, 18/67 responses; multiple responses were possible), funding (22%, n = 15), and interest in development alone (19%, n = 13). 67% (n = 23) declared no or little statistical support. Most (82%, n = 28) did not use their own model in clinical practice and most (56%, n = 19) also believed other clinicians would not use the model either. Most (79%, n = 27) did not use models in general. A substantial proportion (29%, n = 10) reported model development to progress their career via publication. Most respondents had neither evaluated their model nor intended to do so. Most did not use their own model in clinical practice, nor did they believe others would. Statistical assistance was largely absent or minimal. Our data suggest that the large volume of multivariable models currently available in the indexed medical literature have little clinical utility.

The frequency of this allele is higher in individuals of African, Asian (e.g., Han Chinese, Korean, Thai), and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander ancestry. One normal function allele and one increased function allele results in a rapid metabolizer. Therefore, it is advisable to prescribe an increased dose of 150 mg daily for the first month post-PCI followed by a maintenance dose of 75 mg daily thereafter, or consider alternative antiplatelet therapies such as prasugrel or ticagrelor if there are contraindications to higher clopidogrel doses. This adjustment is critical for ensuring effective platelet inhibition and preventing adverse cardiovascular events.

The patient underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and requires clopidogrel as part of their post-PCI treatment regimen.
